Sub-events.Sub-event_summary: General Bradley limited Patton to Dreux, Chartres, and Orléans due to logistical issues, as supply services couldn't keep up with the rapid advance; gasoline and rations were critical shortages threatening to halt operations.

Sub-event_fulltext.Paragraph_58: General Bradley had limited General Patton to Dreux, Chartres, and Orléans primarily because of logistical problems. The essential difficulty was that the supply services did not have enough transportation to keep up with the breakout from the Cotentin and the spectacular momentum of the Allied advance.<sup>[32](https://www.ibiblio.org/hyperwar/USA/USA-E-Breakout/fn28.html#fn32)</sup> It was obvious after the first week in August that the combat gains were outstripping the capacity of the Communications Zone to keep the units adequately supplied. Because of the rapidity of troop movement and the relative paucity of targets, ammunition was less a problem than were gasoline and rations.<sup>[33](https://www.ibiblio.org/hyperwar/USA/USA-E-Breakout/fn28.html#fn33)</sup> Gasoline consumption, which skyrocketed, and ration requirements, which remained constant, threatened to bring operations to a halt.

Sub-Event-Dates: after the first week in August

Sub-events.Sub-event: Air Supply Efforts and Initial Deliveries
Sub-events.Sub-event_summary: Allied commanders turned to air supply to sustain movement; small amounts arrived in early August due to readiness for airborne operations at Orléans and Chartres; after capture, transports less restricted, with first delivery of 47 tons of rations near le Mans on 19 August.

Sub-event_fulltext.Paragraph_59: In order to keep the troops moving, Allied commanders looked to air supply.<sup>[34](https://www.ibiblio.org/hyperwar/USA/USA-E-Breakout/fn28.html#fn34)</sup> Nevertheless, only small amounts of supplies actually arrived on the Continent by air in early August, primarily because transport planes were being held in readiness for possible airborne operations at Orléans and Chartres. Once the two cities were captured, use of the transports was less restricted. On 19 August twenty-one C-47's landed forty-seven tons of rations near le Mans in the first delivery of what was to become a daily emergency airlift to the Third Army.<sup>[35](https://www.ibiblio.org/hyperwar/USA/USA-E-Breakout/fn28.html#fn35)</sup>

Sub-events.Sub-event: Removal of Restrictions and Advance to the Seine
Sub-events.Sub-event_summary: Despite shortages, weak enemy opposition tempted advance; Bradley removed restrictions on 17 August after meeting with Hodges and Patton; advance to Seine would extend Allied trap from Argentan through Chambois to Dreux.

Sub-event_fulltext.Paragraph_60: Although this emergency measure hardly promised to make up all shortages, the temptation to take advantage of the weak enemy opposition at Dreux, Chartres, and Orléans (despite the local resistance at Chartres) was irresistible. After meeting with Hodges and Patton to discuss "spheres of influence" and "zones of action," Bradley on 17 August removed his restriction on going beyond the confines of the Overload lodgment area to the Seine. Since the main enemy forces were concentrated west of the lower Seine (north of Paris), Allied troops advancing to the Seine would in
Sub-event_fulltext.Paragraph_61: effect be extending to the river the lower jaw of the Allied trap, which already stretched from Argentan through Chambois to Dreux.<sup>[36](https://www.ibiblio.org/hyperwar/USA/USA-E-Breakout/fn28.html#fn36)</sup>

Sub-events.Sub-event_summary: To conserve supplies, Patton held XII Corps at Orléans, instructed XX Corps to capture Chartres and assume Dreux responsibility, directed XV Corps to drive to Mantes-Gassicourt to interdict roads and disrupt ferrying.

Sub-event_fulltext.Paragraph_62: To conserve gasoline and other supplies, Patton held the XII Corps at Orléans. He instructed the XX Corps to complete the capture of Chartres and at the same time to assume responsibility for Dreux. He directed the XV Corps to drive twenty-five miles northeast from Dreux to the Seine at Mantes-Gassicourt, a town thirty miles northwest of Paris. At Mantes, the XV Corps was to interdict the roads east of the river and disrupt German ferrying operations.<sup>[37](https://www.ibiblio.org/hyperwar/USA/USA-E-Breakout/fn28.html#fn37)</sup>

Sub-Event-Images: German Removing Boobytrap under the eyes of a U.S. soldier.

Sub-events.Sub-event_summary: 5th Armored and 79th Infantry Divisions relieved at Dreux and Nogent-le-Roi by 7th Armored, moved to Mantes-Gassicourt on 18 August, set up roadblocks and interdiction; on 19 August, task force entered and found Germans gone.

Sub-event_fulltext.Paragraph_63: The 5th Armored and 79th Infantry Divisions of the XV Corps, relieved at Dreux and Nogent-le-Roi by the 7th Armored Division, moved easily to Mantes-Gassicourt on 18 August, set up roadblocks to collect German stragglers, and placed interdictory artillery fire on the river-crossing sites. On the following day a task force of the 79th entered Mantes-Gassicourt and found the Germans gone.

Sub-events.Sub-event_summary: On 19 August, as XV Corps found no obstacle at Seine, Allied commanders agreed to move directly into post-OVERLORD operations toward Germany instead of halting at Seine for reorganization.

Sub-event_fulltext.Paragraph_64: On 19 August, while the XV Corps was discovering that no effective obstacle save the river itself barred a crossing of the Seine, the top Allied commanders were reaching agreement to modify further the OVERLORD planning. Instead of halting at the Seine to reorganize and build up a supply base west of the Seine, the Allied command decided to move immediately into post-OVERLORD operations directed toward Germany.<sup>[38](https://www.ibiblio.org/hyperwar/USA/USA-E-Breakout/fn28.html#fn38)</sup>

Sub-events.Sub-event: Opportunity for Encirclement West of the Seine
Sub-events.Sub-event_summary: Driving across upper and lower Seine simple, but Germans between pocket and lower Seine offered encirclement opportunity; estimated 75,000 troops and 250 tanks could be encircled west of Seine.

Sub-event_fulltext.Paragraph_65: To drive across the upper Seine south of Paris and the lower Seine north of Paris would be a comparatively simple maneuver, but the presence of a considerable number of Germans between the Argentan-Falaise pocket and the lower Seine presented an opportunity to complete the destruction of the forces that had escaped the pocket. The Allies estimated that 75,000 enemy troops and 250 tanks could still be encircled west of the Seine.<sup>[39](https://www.ibiblio.org/hyperwar/USA/USA-E-Breakout/fn28.html#fn39)</sup> If American troops drove down the west bank of the Seine from Mantes-Gassicourt, they might cut German escape routes, push the Germans toward the mouth of the Seine, where the river is wider and more difficult
Sub-event_fulltext.Paragraph_66: to cross, and fashion another encirclement inside Normandy.

Sub-events.Sub-event: Challenges of Maneuver Down West Bank
Sub-events.Sub-event_summary: Main difficulty was XV Corps beyond 12th Army Group zone; further advance would cross British and Canadian routes, causing administrative issues.

Sub-event_fulltext.Paragraph_67: The major difficulty of a maneuver such as this was the same that had inhibited American activity north of Argentan. At Mantes, the XV Corps was again beyond the zone assigned to the 12 th Army Group. Further advance toward the mouth of the Seine would place the corps across the projected routes of advance of the British and Canadian armies and would surely result in "an administrative headache."<sup>[40](https://www.ibiblio.org/hyperwar/USA/USA-E-Breakout/fn28.html#fn40)</sup>

Sub-events.Sub-event_summary: Bradley offered trucks for British troops, suggested movement through American zone; Dempsey declined due to logistics; to exploit opportunities, Montgomery permitted American intrusion into British sector, accepting administrative consequences.

Sub-event_fulltext.Paragraph_68: Although General Bradley offered to lend trucks to transport British troops to Mantes-Gassicourt and suggested that the British move units through the American zone to launch the attack down the west bank of the river, General Dempsey declined with thanks on the basis that his logistical organization could not support such a move. For the Allies then to take advantage of the alluring possibilities at the Seine--disrupting the German withdrawal, bagging additional prisoners among the escapees from the Argentan-Falaise pocket, removing Germans from the British zone, and thus allowing Dempsey to move to the Seine against "almost negligible resistance"--General Montgomery would have to permit further intrusion of American troops into the British sector and accept in advance the administrative consequences. He, Bradley, and Dempsey decided to chance the headache.<sup>[41](https://www.ibiblio.org/hyperwar/USA/USA-E-Breakout/fn28.html#fn41)</sup>

Sub-events.Sub-event: Double Mission for XV Corps and Montgomery's Order
Sub-events.Sub-event_summary: Decided to send part of Patton's force down west bank, seize east bank bridgehead; XV Corps: 5th Armored down west bank, 79th bridgehead east; Montgomery's order on 20 August urged record time finish.

Sub-event_fulltext.Paragraph_69: Having decided to send part of Patton's force down the west bank of the Seine, the Allied commanders saw a coincident opportunity to seize a bridgehead on the east bank of the river as a springboard for future operations. The XV Corps thus drew a double mission-- the 5th Armored was to attack down the west bank while the 79th established a bridgehead on the east bank. In his order issued on 20 August, Montgomery cautioned: "This is no time to relax, or to sit back and congratulate ourselves. . . . Let us finish off the business in record time."<sup>[42](https://www.ibiblio.org/hyperwar/USA/USA-E-Breakout/fn28.html#fn42)</sup> By then, American troops were already across the Seine.

Sub-events.Sub-event_summary: General Wyche received order at 2135 on 19 August from Haislip to cross Seine that night: foot troops east bank, build bridge, gain depth to protect from artillery.

Sub-event_fulltext.Paragraph_70: General Wyche had received a telephone call at 2135, 19 August, from General Haislip, who ordered him to cross the Seine that night.<sup>[43](https://www.ibiblio.org/hyperwar/USA/USA-E-Breakout/fn28.html#fn43)</sup> The 79th was to get foot troops on the east bank at once, build a bridge for vehicles, tanks, and heavy equipment, and gain ground in sufficient depth (four to six miles) to protect the crossing sites at Mantes from medium artillery fire.

Sub-events.Sub-event_summary: Situation fluid, anticipated little resistance; 79th engaged scattered groups, captured vehicles and tank, received sporadic fire; Seine 500-800 feet wide near Mantes; dam offered foot path, assault boats for others; secured 700 feet treadway from 5th Armored.

Sub-event_fulltext.Paragraph_71: In a situation that was "too fluid to define an enemy front line," General Wyche anticipated little resistance. His 79th Division had that day engaged only scattered German groups in flight, had captured nineteen vehicles and a Mark IV tank, and had received only sporadic machine gun fire from across the Seine. The river itself was the main problem, for near Mantes it varied in width from five hundred to eight hundred feet.
Sub-event_fulltext.Paragraph_72: Fortunately, a dam nearby offered a narrow foot path across it, and Engineer assault boats and rafts could transport other troops and light equipment. For the bridge he was to build, Wyche secured seven hundred feet of treadway from the 5th Armored Division.

Sub-events.Sub-event_summary: During rain night of 19 August, 313th Infantry crossed dam single file; at daybreak 20 August, 314th paddled across, engineers installed treadway; afternoon, 315th crossed in trucks; by nightfall, bulk of division including tanks and artillery on east bank.

Sub-event_fulltext.Paragraph_73: While a torrential rain fell during the night of 19 August, men of the 313th Infantry walked across the dam in single file, each man touching the one ahead to keep from falling into the water. At daybreak, 20 August, as the 314th Infantry paddled across the river, the division engineers began to install the treadway. In the afternoon, as soon as the bridge was ready, the 315th Infantry crossed in trucks. By nightfall, 20 August, the bulk of the division, including tanks, artillery, and tank destroyers, was on the east bank. The following day battalions of the XV Corps Artillery crossed. Antiaircraft units hurriedly emplaced their pieces around the bridge, arriving in time to shoot down about a dozen enemy planes on the first day and to amass a total of almost fifty claimed in four days. To supplement the treadway, engineers constructed a Bailey bridge that was opened to traffic on 23 August. On the east bank, the 79th not only extended and improved the bridgehead, repelled counterattacks, and placed interdiction on highways, ferry routes, and barge traffic lanes, but also dramatically pointed out to the Germans their critical situation by capturing the *Army Group B* command post at la Roche-Guyon and sending the German headquarters troops scurrying eastward to Soissons.<sup>[44](https://www.ibiblio.org/hyperwar/USA/USA-E-Breakout/fn28.html#fn44)</sup>
